opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. Honestly, what surprised me most is *where* the generalization came from. For a long time in robotics, we assumed that to get a robot to do a new task, you had to collect data for that task: teleoperate it hundreds or thousands of times, tune the reward, engineer the environment. Generalization was something we hoped for but rarely saw. If you moved a cup ten centimeters, or changed the lighting, the policy would often just fall apart.

What changed is that once we started building robot models on top of large vision-language models, a lot of that generalization came almost for free. The model already knows what a "banana" is, what "the leftmost object" means, what "put it in the bin with the matching color" implies. The robot data teaches it how to move, but the semantic understanding, the common sense, transfers from internet-scale pretraining. The first time I saw a robot correctly handle an instruction involving an object it had never seen in any of our robot data, I was genuinely shocked. It felt like the model understood the task rather than memorizing a trajectory.

The second surprise is cross-embodiment transfer. We used to think each robot was its own island: data from one arm wasn't useful for another arm with different kinematics. But when you pool data across many different robots and train one model, performance on each individual robot often goes *up*. That runs against the old intuition, and it suggests there's a shared structure to physical interaction that these models can pick up.

That said, I want to be careful not to overstate it. Semantic generalization, understanding *what* to do, has improved dramatically. Physical generalization, actually doing it robustly with the right forces, in clutter, with deformable objects, over long horizons, is still much harder. A robot might understand "fold the shirt" perfectly and still fumble the actual folding. So the gap has shifted: the bottleneck used to be understanding, and now it's increasingly dexterity and reliability. That's where I think a lot of the exciting work is right now.

r001.rationale: The response describes handling an unseen object and transfer across different robots, but does not identify successful task execution on a previously unseen control device.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, what surprised me most is how much of the generalization came from the data and the model rather than from the robot itself. For years, those of us in robot learning assumed that if you wanted a robot to do something new, you had to go collect data for that specific thing, in that specific environment, and train for it. The gap between "works in the lab" and "works in a kitchen it has never seen" felt like a fundamental barrier.

What changed is that we started treating robot learning more like language modeling. When you pretrain on large and diverse datasets, and especially when you bring in vision-language models that have already seen the whole internet, the robot inherits a kind of common sense about objects and scenes. So you can say "put the apple next to the red cup," and even if that exact combination never appeared in the training data, the model has a reasonable idea of what an apple is, what red means, and what "next to" implies. That semantic generalization caught me off guard. I expected it to be brittle, and it was much less brittle than I thought.

The second surprise is the role of simulation and cross-embodiment data. We used to worry a lot about the sim-to-real gap and about data from one robot not transferring to another. It turns out that if you have enough variety, the model learns to abstract away a lot of those differences. A policy trained on a mix of arms and even humanoids can be surprisingly adaptable, and simulation is useful not because it is perfectly realistic, but because it lets you cover a huge range of situations cheaply.

That said, I want to be careful not to oversell it. The generalization is strong at the level of understanding the task, but it is still weaker at the level of physical skill. A robot can understand "fold the shirt" much more easily than it can actually fold the shirt reliably across different fabrics. Contact-rich manipulation, dexterity, recovering gracefully from mistakes, those remain hard. So the surprise, for me, is really about how far semantic and visual understanding has come. The physical side is moving, but it is moving at a more traditional, step-by-step pace.

r001.rationale: The response says policies trained across different robot embodiments can be adaptable, but it does not identify successful task execution on a previously unseen control device as evidence of generalization.

astra-6.text:
What has surprised me most is how much a robot can bring to a new task before we train it specifically for that task. Traditionally, we would build a system for one particular behavior, and even a small change in the environment could cause it to fail. Now we’re starting to see systems that can take a familiar skill and apply it to an unfamiliar object, or interpret an instruction they haven’t encountered in exactly that form.

I think a particularly interesting part is the connection between semantic understanding and physical behavior. Knowing what an object is, or what a person wants, helps enormously. But knowing what to do is still different from knowing how to move your hand, make contact, and recover when something slips.

So I’m excited by the breadth of what’s becoming possible. The question I’d still ask is: how reliably does it work? A robot succeeding once on an unfamiliar task is exciting. A robot succeeding consistently, and recognizing when it needs help—that’s a much higher bar.

r001.rationale: The response discusses applying familiar skills to unfamiliar objects and instructions, but it does not identify successful execution on a previously unseen control device.

sol-6.1.text:
What surprises me most is that we’re starting to see robots reuse what they’ve learned instead of learning every task from scratch. A new object or a slightly different instruction doesn’t always require a completely new training process. That’s an exciting shift.

But I think we have to be careful about what we mean by generalization. Handling a different-looking object is one thing; recovering when it slips, or figuring out what to do when the environment changes, is much harder. For me, the interesting question is becoming less “Can the robot do this once?” and more “Can it do this reliably, and recover when something goes wrong?”

r001.rationale: The response discusses reusing learned skills for new objects or instructions, but does not identify successful task execution on a previously unseen control device.
